Statement I: cis-2-butene is \(CH_{3}CH=CHCH_{3}\). Reductive ozonolysis (\(O_{3}\), then \(Zn/H_{2}O\)) cleaves the double bond into two carbonyl fragments, each \(CH_{3}CHO\). So ethanal is indeed the product and Statement I is TRUE.

Statement II: 3,6-dimethyloct-4-ene is \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH(CH_{3})-CH=CH-CH(CH_{3})CH_{2}CH_{3}\). Ozonolysis cleaves the C4=C5 bond, giving two identical molecules of 2-methylbutanal, \(OHC-CH(CH_{3})-CH_{2}CH_{3}\). The carbon bearing the methyl group now carries four different groups: \(-CHO\), \(-CH_{3}\), \(-C_{2}H_{5}\) and \(-H\); it is therefore a chiral carbon. The claim that the product has no chiral carbon is FALSE.

Let the initial pressure of pure A be \(P_{0}\) and let \(x\) be the pressure of A consumed at time t.
\(A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g) + C(g)\)
At time t: \(p_{A} = P_{0}-x\), \(p_{B} = 2x\), \(p_{C} = x\), so \(P_{total} = P_{0}+2x\).

At \(t = \infty\), \(x = P_{0}\): \(P_{\infty} = 3P_{0} = 240\) so \(P_{0} = 80\) mm Hg. Option (A) is correct.

At \(t = 10\) min: \(80 + 2x = 160\) gives \(x = 40\), hence \(p_{A} = 80-40 = 40\) mm Hg. Option (D) is correct.

Rate constant: \(k = \frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{P_{0}}{p_{A}} = \frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{80}{40} = \frac{0.693}{10} = 0.0693\ \min^{-1}\), not \(1.693\ \min^{-1}\). Option (C) is INCORRECT.

Option (B) is a correct statement: for a first order reaction the concentration falls exponentially and reaches zero only as \(t \rightarrow \infty\).

Build a three-step path from \(H_{2}O(l)\) at \(10^{\circ}C\) to \(H_{2}O(s)\) at \(-10^{\circ}C\) and add the enthalpies (Hess's law). Work in joules, noting \(\Delta_{fus}H = x\) kJ/mol \(= 1000x\) J/mol while y and z are in \(J\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}\).

Step 1, cool the liquid \(10^{\circ}C \rightarrow 0^{\circ}C\): \(\Delta H_{1} = y(0-10) = -10y\) J.
Step 2, freeze at \(0^{\circ}C\) (reverse of fusion): \(\Delta H_{2} = -1000x\) J.
Step 3, cool the ice \(0^{\circ}C \rightarrow -10^{\circ}C\): \(\Delta H_{3} = z(-10-0) = -10z\) J.

Total \(= -1000x - 10y - 10z = -10\left(100x + y + z\right)\) J.

The figure is the visible spectrum from 400 nm (violet) to 750 nm (red), and the premise is that yellow light already ejects electrons from caesium, i.e. the frequency of yellow light exceeds the threshold frequency of Cs.

A. Current flows with yellow light. Given as the premise, CORRECT.
B. Photocurrent is proportional to the number of incident photons, so dimming the yellow light reduces the current (it does not change the kinetic energy of the electrons). CORRECT.
B'/C. Red light has a longer wavelength and therefore a LOWER frequency than yellow. Since yellow is only just above threshold, red lies below the threshold frequency and no photoelectrons are emitted at all - the current cannot be higher. INCORRECT.
D. Blue light has a higher frequency than yellow, so emission occurs. CORRECT.
E. White light contains blue, green and yellow components which are above threshold, so a current is produced. CORRECT.

Correct statements: A, B, D and E.

First ionisation enthalpies in group 14 (kJ/mol): \(C = 1086\), \(Si = 786\), \(Ge = 761\), \(Sn = 708\), \(Pb = 715\). The two lowest values, 708 and 715, identify \(A = Sn\) and \(B = Pb\).

Because of the inert pair effect the \(+2\) state becomes more stable down the group:
- For tin the stable state is \(+4\), so \(Sn^{2+}\) readily loses two more electrons and acts as a REDUCING agent (\(Sn^{2+} \rightarrow Sn^{4+} + 2e^{-}\)).
- For lead the stable state is \(+2\), so \(Pb^{4+}\) readily accepts electrons and acts as an OXIDISING agent (\(Pb^{4+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Pb^{2+}\)).

Hence \(A^{2+}\) is reducing and \(B^{4+}\) is oxidising.

Enthalpies of atomisation of the 3d series peak at vanadium (\(515\) kJ/mol), higher than Ti (473), Cr (397), Fe (418), Co (425) and Ni (430). So \(M = V\).

Among the aquated vanadium ions, \(V^{2+}\) is violet, \(\left[V\left(H_{2}O\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}\) is green, \(VO^{2+}\) is blue and \(VO_{2}^{+}\) is yellow. The green aquated ion is therefore \(V^{3+}\).

The oxide corresponding to \(V^{3+}\) is \(V_{2}O_{3}\). In a transition series the oxide becomes more acidic as the oxidation state rises; at the low \(+3\) state \(V_{2}O_{3}\) is BASIC (it dissolves in acids to give \(V^{3+}\) salts). Higher oxides such as \(VO_{2}\) are amphoteric and \(V_{2}O_{5}\) is largely acidic.

Sodium bicarbonate liberates \(CO_{2}\) only from acids stronger than carbonic acid (\(pK_{a1} \approx 6.4\)):
\(RCOOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow RCOONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2} \uparrow\)

A. Picric acid, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: three nitro groups delocalise the phenoxide charge so strongly that \(pK_{a} \approx 0.4\). It is far stronger than \(H_{2}CO_{3}\), effervescence occurs.
B. 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, \(pK_{a} \approx 3.4\), a carboxylic acid, effervescence occurs.
C. Anilinium chloride, \(C_{6}H_{5}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}\), \(pK_{a} \approx 4.6\) for the anilinium ion, still more acidic than carbonic acid, so \(CO_{2}\) is released.
D. 3-Nitrophenol, \(pK_{a} \approx 8.4\). A single meta nitro group offers only an inductive pull (no direct resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide from the meta position), so it remains a WEAKER acid than carbonic acid and cannot displace \(CO_{2}\) from bicarbonate.

Hence D is least likely to give effervescence.

Before the medicine: growth is first order in the bacterial population, \(\frac{dN}{dt} = kN\), so \(N = N_{0}e^{kt}\) and \(\frac{N}{N_{0}} = e^{kt}\). The plot of \(N/N_{0}\) against t must therefore START AT 1 at \(t = 0\) and rise exponentially.

After the medicine: the stem states the rate of decay is proportional to the square of the number of bacteria, \(r = kN^{2}\). A plot of r against N is therefore a parabola passing through the origin, rising with increasing steepness (not linear, not decreasing).

Option A fails because its r-versus-N curve falls with N.
Option C fails because its 'before' curve starts from \(N/N_{0} = 0\) rather than 1.
Option D fails because its r-versus-N plot is a straight line, i.e. first order in N.
Option B alone shows \(N/N_{0}\) starting at 1 and rising exponentially, together with a concave-up parabolic \(r\) versus \(N\) curve through the origin.

Statement I: Sucrose is made from D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose. Fructose is LAEVOROTATORY, so writing the hydrolysis products (and the condensation partners) as D-(+)-glucose and D-(+)-fructose is wrong. Statement I is FALSE.

Statement II: Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory (\(+66.5^{\circ}\)). On hydrolysis it gives D-(+)-glucose (\(+52.5^{\circ}\)) and D-(-)-fructose (\(-92.4^{\circ}\)); the strongly laevorotatory fructose dominates, so the mixture is laevorotatory and the sign of rotation is INVERTED. Isomer A gives a white precipitate with \(AgNO_{3}\), so it releases free chloride ion in solution: the chloride is OUTSIDE the coordination sphere and sulphate is coordinated, i.e. \(\left[Co\left(NH_{3}\right)_{5}SO_{4}\right]Cl\).

Isomer B gives a white precipitate with \(BaCl_{2}\), so it releases free sulphate ion: the sulphate is OUTSIDE the sphere and chloride is coordinated, i.e. \(\left[Co\left(NH_{3}\right)_{5}Cl\right]SO_{4}\).

The two isomers have the same overall composition but interchange a ligand inside the coordination sphere with the counter-ion outside it, producing different ions in solution. This is IONISATION isomerism.

It is not coordination isomerism (that needs both a complex cation and a complex anion), not linkage isomerism (no ambidentate ligand switching donor atoms) and not geometrical isomerism (that would not change the precipitation behaviour).

Take each reaction from the figures.

A. 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane with \(NaOEt\) (a strong alkoxide base in alcohol) undergoes E2 dehydrohalogenation to give methylcyclohexene. Alkene IS formed.

First find the ion concentrations left after electrolysis.

Copper half-cell: 1 F = 1 mol of electrons; \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu\) needs 2 F per mole, so 0.5 mol of \(Cu^{2+}\) is deposited. Starting with \(1.5\ M \times 1\ L = 1.5\) mol, the remainder is \(1.5 - 0.5 = 1.0\) mol in 1 L, i.e. \(\left[Cu^{2+}\right] = 1.0\) M.

Silver half-cell: 0.1 F deposits 0.1 mol of Ag (\(Ag^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Ag\)). Starting with 0.2 mol, the remainder is \(0.2 - 0.1 = 0.1\) mol in 1 L, i.e. \(\left[Ag^{+}\right] = 0.1\) M.

On joining the two half-cells (figure shows Cu and Ag electrodes with a salt bridge and a meter), silver has the higher reduction potential, so Cu is the anode and Ag the cathode:
\(Cu\left(s\right) + 2Ag^{+} \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2Ag\left(s\right)\), \(n = 2\).

\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.80 - 0.34 = 0.46\ V\)

\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \frac{0.06}{n}\log\frac{\left[Cu^{2+}\right]}{\left[Ag^{+}\right]^{2}} = 0.46 - \frac{0.06}{2}\log\frac{1.0}{\left(0.1\right)^{2}}\)

\(= 0.46 - 0.03 \times \log 100 = 0.46 - 0.06 = 0.40\ V = 400 \times 10^{-3}\ V\).

Aqueous 5 M NaOH extracts only those components that form a water-soluble salt with a strong base.

Benzoic acid is acidic and is converted to sodium benzoate:
\(C_{6}H_{5}COOH + NaOH \rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}COO^{-}Na^{+} + H_{2}O\), which is ionic and passes into the AQUEOUS layer.

Aniline is a base, not an acid, so NaOH cannot deprotonate it; it stays in the organic ethyl acetate layer. (It would be extracted by dilute HCl, not NaOH.)

Chlorobenzene is neutral and remains in the organic layer.

Hence the ethyl acetate layer retains chlorobenzene and aniline.

Dissolution is treated as a two-step Hess cycle: break the lattice into gaseous ions, then hydrate them.

Step 1, \(KCl\left(s\right) \rightarrow K^{+}\left(g\right) + Cl^{-}\left(g\right)\). The lattice enthalpy (formation of the lattice from gaseous ions) is \(-z\), so the reverse process costs \(+z\).

Step 2, hydration: \(K^{+}\left(g\right) \rightarrow K^{+}\left(aq\right)\) releases \(-x\) and \(Cl^{-}\left(g\right) \rightarrow Cl^{-}\left(aq\right)\) releases \(-y\).

\(\Delta H_{solution} = z + \left(-x\right) + \left(-y\right) = z - \left(x + y\right)\).

Let the initial pressure of A be \(P_{0}\) and let \(x\) be the pressure of A consumed at time t.
\(A\left(g\right) \rightarrow B\left(g\right) + C\left(g\right)\)
At time t: \(p_{A} = P_{0} - x\), \(p_{B} = p_{C} = x\), so \(P_{t} = P_{0} + x\).

At \(t = \infty\) all of A has reacted (\(x = P_{0}\)), so \(P_{\infty} = 2P_{0}\), giving \(P_{0} = \frac{P_{\infty}}{2}\).

Then \(x = P_{t} - P_{0} = P_{t} - \frac{P_{\infty}}{2}\) and
\(p_{A} = P_{0} - x = \frac{P_{\infty}}{2} - \left(P_{t} - \frac{P_{\infty}}{2}\right) = P_{\infty} - P_{t}\).

For a first order reaction,
\(k = \frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{P_{0}}{p_{A}} = \frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{P_{\infty}/2}{P_{\infty} - P_{t}} = \frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{P_{\infty}}{2\left(P_{\infty} - P_{t}\right)}\).

The tests fix the functional group: a positive 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine test means a carbonyl group is present, while a NEGATIVE Tollens test rules out an aldehyde. So P is a KETONE of formula \(C_{6}H_{12}O\), and it must also be optically active, i.e. carry a stereocentre.

A. \(CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{3}\), hexan-2-one: a ketone, but no carbon bears four different groups, so it is achiral.
B. \(CH_{3}COCH\left(CH_{3}\right)CH_{2}CH_{3}\), 3-methylpentan-2-one: a ketone; C-3 carries \(-COCH_{3}\), \(-CH_{3}\), \(-C_{2}H_{5}\) and \(-H\), four different groups, so it IS chiral and optically active. Fits every clue.
C. \(OHC-CH_{2}CH\left(CH_{3}\right)CH_{2}CH_{3}\), 3-methylpentanal: an aldehyde, so it would give a POSITIVE Tollens test. Ruled out.
D. \(CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH\left(CH_{3}\right)_{2}\), 4-methylpentan-2-one: a ketone, but C-4 carries two identical methyl groups, so it is achiral.

Structure P is B.

Nucleophilic substitution on an aryl halide proceeds through a Meisenheimer intermediate whose negative charge must be delocalised onto electron-withdrawing groups ortho or para to the halogen. The more such nitro groups are present, the milder the conditions required.

(A) Chlorobenzene to phenol: no activating group at all, so the forcing Dow conditions are needed - \(NaOH\) at 623 K and 300 atm, then \(H_{3}O^{+}\). This is (IV).
(B) 4-Nitrochlorobenzene to 4-nitrophenol: one para nitro group, so \(NaOH\) at 443 K suffices. This is (III).
(C) 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene to 2,4-dinitrophenol: two activating nitro groups, so warm \(NaOH\) at 368 K is enough. This is (II).
(D) 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene (picryl chloride) to picric acid: three nitro groups make the ring so electron-poor that simple warm water hydrolyses it. This is (I).

A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

Complete ozonolysis cleaves all three carbon-carbon double bonds. The fragments are:

Examine each proposed reason for the extra stability of exactly half-filled and completely filled subshells.

(A) Symmetrical distribution of electrons - CORRECT. A half-filled or fully filled subshell has its electron density distributed symmetrically over the degenerate orbitals, and symmetry lowers the energy. This is one of the two reasons stated in the standard text.

(B) Smaller coulombic repulsion energy - CORRECT. In a half-filled subshell every orbital holds a single electron, so no pairing energy is paid and the electron-electron repulsion is minimised.

(C) The presence of electrons with the same spin in NON-DEGENERATE orbitals - INCORRECT. Exchange stabilisation arises when two or more electrons of the same spin occupy DEGENERATE orbitals of the same subshell and can exchange positions. Replacing 'degenerate' by 'non-degenerate' makes the statement chemically wrong.

(D) Larger exchange energy - CORRECT. The number of possible exchanges is a maximum for a half-filled or completely filled subshell, so the exchange energy released is a maximum.

(E) Relatively smaller shielding of electrons by one another - CORRECT. Electrons of parallel spin keep apart (the Fermi hole), so they screen the nucleus from one another less effectively; the resulting higher effective nuclear charge binds them more tightly.

Correct statements: (A), (B), (D) and (E) only.
